front: Which three blocks are RFC 1918 private space?
What is the last address inside RFC 1918 block 172.16.0.0/12?
back: 172.31.255.255. An address beginning 172.32 is outside that private block.

front: How do /20, /26, and octet-aligned /24 boundaries differ?
back: /20 varies within the third octet; /26 within the fourth. /24 has three full network octets and one full host octet.

front: How do you count equal-size child subnets and usable addresses?
back: Parent /p to child /q: 2^(q−p) subnets. Each ordinary child through /30: 2^(32−q) − 2 usable addresses.

front: What checks make a VLSM allocation valid?
back: Enough capacity, correct boundary, containment in the parent, and no overlap. Allocate larger blocks first in empty space.

front: How do you find a single containing summary?
back: Find the shared leading bits of the full address range. Use them as the prefix and clear the remaining bits; check extra covered space.

front: Why can’t 10.44.9.0/24 through 10.44.12.0/24 form one exact /22?
back: They straddle the /22 boundary between third-octet values 11 and 12. The smallest containing /21 also covers extra /24s.

front: What does an automatically assigned 169.254.x.x address suggest?
back: IPv4 link-local fallback. Investigate why normal DHCP configuration was not obtained; the address alone does not identify the cause.

front: Do modern subnet counts exclude subnet zero and the all-ones subnet?
back: No. All 2^s subnet numbers are available after adding s prefix bits. Do not confuse this with reserving host network/broadcast addresses.

front: Which IPv4 blocks identify loopback and multicast addresses?
back: 127.0.0.0/8 is loopback; 224.0.0.0/4 is multicast. Neither is ordinary unicast addressing for a workstation LAN.
0.0.0.0 can mean unspecified; 0.0.0.0/0 is the default-route prefix. 255.255.255.255 is the limited broadcast.

front: How do invalid host addresses differ from overlapping allocations?
back: Network/broadcast selection makes the host address unsuitable. Overlap means two proposed routed subnet ranges share addresses; inspect the relevant masks.

front: What should you verify when local pings work but remote pings fail?
back: Both endpoints' masks and gateways, followed by router routes. A too-wide mask can make remote addresses appear local.

front: Can nonoverlapping RFC 1918 LANs communicate through ordinary internal routing?
back: Yes. Appropriate routes and usable paths can connect them without NAT; private addressing does not itself block forwarding.

front: What distinguishes FLSM from VLSM?
back: FLSM uses one child-subnet size; VLSM uses different sizes to suit separate requirements. Both still require valid, nonoverlapping allocations.

front: What must an addressed-interface requirement include before you choose a subnet size?
back: Count end devices, router interfaces and any stated growth or reservations. Do not add a gateway twice when the given total already includes it.

front: How do you choose the smallest ordinary subnet for a usable-address requirement?
back: Choose the fewest host bits h for which 2^h − 2 meets the requirement, then use prefix 32 − h. Check placement separately.

front: What happens to capacity when a prefix grows from /26 to /27?
back: The address block halves from 64 to 32 total addresses; ordinary usable capacity drops from 62 to 30. A longer prefix cannot fix a capacity shortage.

front: Why can 128 free addresses still fail to provide a /26?
back: The addresses may be split into gaps. A /26 requires one aligned, contiguous 64-address block with no occupied addresses inside.

front: What proves that a proposed subnet is contained in its approved parent?
back: Its entire network-to-broadcast range lies within the parent. Checking only the gateway or the first few octets is insufficient.

front: How do you choose gateway and test-host addresses after allocating a LAN?
back: Choose distinct usable addresses in that subnet, reserve the router’s address, and give each host the matching mask and actual local gateway.

front: Does changing a router interface’s address or mask update static PC settings?
back: No. Update and verify the affected PCs separately against the new allocation. Check their address, mask and gateway.

front: When does allocating largest first simplify VLSM placement?
back: In an empty contiguous parent. Existing assignments still require checking the actual free intervals; sorting requirements does not remove fragmentation.

front: What should a small subnet-renumbering verification record include?
back: The new router prefix, each changed PC’s settings, local gateway tests and both directions to unchanged LANs. Test the new addresses, not the retired ones.
